chapter_title: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
learning_objective: The learner will judge the strength of the evidence behind ten vendor claims by assigning each to one of five evidence levels, correctly placing at least eight of ten on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** evidence-tier-claim-checker
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** judge
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge the strength of the evidence behind ten vendor claims by assigning each to one of five evidence levels, correctly placing at least eight of ten on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** evidence-based practice, randomized controlled trial, selection bias, the five evidence levels (Strong, Moderate, Promising, Demonstrates a rationale, No evidence of effect), all defined in the section "Evidence-Based Practice: Judging What Works" above. **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of 10 claims in one of five level bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct level" column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A large sample makes a claim strong whatever the study design. (2) Teacher satisfaction is evidence of learning. (3) Any before-and-after gain shows the program worked. **Instructional Rationale:** Judging is an Evaluate-level act: the learner must apply criteria (how groups were formed) to unfamiliar claims and commit to a verdict. Including a very large self-selected sample and a before-and-after gain forces the learner to rely on design, not on impressive-sounding numbers. **Content:** Five bins, each with its one-line definition shown on request: | Bin | Definition shown | |---|---| | Strong | Random assignment, well designed and well carried out | | Moderate | A comparison group, but no random assignment | | Promising | A correlational study that adjusts for who chose the program | | Demonstrates a rationale | A research-based reason to expect it to work; results not yet in | | No evidence of effect | Testimonials, surveys, usage counts, uncontrolled before-and-after or self-selected comparisons | Ten claims about the fictional program "MathPath": | # | Claim shown to the learner | Correct level | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | "In a study where 1,200 students were randomly assigned to MathPath or a control group, the MathPath group gained 0.15 standard deviations more on the state test." | Strong | Random assignment and a standardized outcome measure. | | 2 | "A district compared 800 MathPath students with 800 matched students who did not use it, matched on prior scores and demographics; MathPath students gained more." | Moderate | There is a comparison group, but it was chosen, not drawn by lot. | | 3 | "Across 40 schools, students who used MathPath more hours scored higher, after statistical adjustment for prior scores and family income." | Promising | A correlational study with controls; it still cannot rule out unmeasured differences. | | 4 | "MathPath's design is based on research about spaced and retrieval practice, and an independent evaluation is under way." | Demonstrates a rationale | A research-based reason to expect it to work, with results still to come. | | 5 | "94% of teachers surveyed said they love MathPath." | No evidence of effect | A satisfaction survey does not measure learning. | | 6 | "Students in one pilot classroom raised their average score by 12 points from fall to spring." | No evidence of effect | Students usually gain over a school year; with no comparison group the gain cannot be credited to the program. | | 7 | "Among 12,000 students, those who chose to use the optional MathPath program scored higher than those who did not." | No evidence of effect | Students who choose a program differ from those who do not, and a large sample does not fix that. | | 8 | "Two separate randomized trials in different states, with 2,000 students in total, found gains of 0.10 and 0.18 standard deviations." | Strong | Repeated random-assignment results strengthen the case. | | 9 | "A state analysis compared the 30 schools that adopted MathPath with 30 similar schools that did not, using the same tests." | Moderate | A comparison group of similar schools, but not randomly formed. | | 10 | "MathPath uses mastery learning, which has strong research support in general; no study of MathPath itself has been done." | Demonstrates a rationale | A sound reason to expect results, but no evidence yet about this product. | **Provenance:** The five levels follow the chapter section "Evidence-Based Practice: Judging What Works," which summarizes the Every Student Succeeds Act evidence tiers and adds one bin for non-evidence. The claims are illustrative, written for this chapter; the sim must label them "Fictional claims about a fictional program." **Rules:** Each claim has exactly one correct level, given in Content. A claim is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 10. Mastery is a score >= 8. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads one claim at a time and sees the five bins. 2. The learner places the claim in a bin and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 3. If incorrect, the learner may place the claim again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown. 4. After all 10 claims, the sim shows the score and lists any misplaced claims with their correct levels. 5. The learner should notice that claim 7, with 12,000 students, sits in the lowest bin while claim 1, with 1,200, sits in the highest. **Feedback:** 10 claims, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [level]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the claim counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 10" is shown. Final message for a score >= 8: "You can judge a claim by how its comparison was built." For a score < 8: "Review the level definitions and try again; the claims will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** Claim 1 of the shuffled order is shown with five empty bins and the score "First-try correct: 0 of 10." The prompt reads "How strong is the evidence behind this claim?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter names five evidence levels in the order Strong, Moderate, Promising, Demonstrates a rationale, No evidence of effect. The chapter states that a large sample does not fix self-selection and that satisfaction surveys do not measure learning. The mastery bar is 8 of 10.
